Did you approach -- in other words, perhaps the question was a bit lengthy, but did you approach Buza or Zejnilagic on this topic, bearing in mind that they had identified by number this report which you say you'd never signed?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see even the things they signed later, after this document, but I'll try to answer chronologically to your question. They must have invoked this document or another document bearing the same number, because this is a handwritten number, so it must have been an authentic document. I'm not going to call into question it authenticity. They could have referred to a number of 001/something, ending in "37." But how could I have approached them on this topic if unfortunate as it is - and it's really an insult to me that I had to come here 10, 15 years later to find certain things out for the first time - so how could I have approached them on this topic if I hadn't seen this before? I was unable to ask them why they did something or why they decided the way they decided if I wasn't aware of it. This is the first time I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I saw this order by Zejnilagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why? Because I had never seen that document. I never saw the document invoking the corps order. And unfortunately, it was from the media that I found out that there had been a massacre up there, and I talked about it to Buza. But I didn't have a report. There was in fact a report which contained no more than a paragraph. It was a report written by Buza relating to the casualties, losses that he inflicted on the enemy in heavy fighting. But I was aware that Buza was participating in combat activities at the forward command post of Jablanica together with General Halilovic. That much I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I offer that document for tender. I think I did that already, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is it the right time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before leaving that document, could I put a question to this witness, Mr. Morrissey

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, on the front page, the first page of this document, there is also a signature. In the English version, is that also written by somebody. Witness, do you recognize what is this signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm with certainty to whom it belongs, but it is not unsimilar to the signature of my deputy. However, I could not confirm that it is his signature. It does look like it though. I see it, for instance, in the letter "F," but I cannot claim for sure. I cannot say positively it is my deputy's signature. I can only suppose it could be his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: According to the rules, generally speaking who will sign there? Who has power to sign there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should have signed this if it was an order of a unit subordinate to me. But you cannot see from the preamble to which unit it is directed, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina-6 Corps. Below that it should have stated "Corps command" or maybe "317th Brigade" or "The Independent Prozor Battalion." So this third line is missing. If it had been corps command, then I would have been the one who was supposed to approve, to endorse this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Morrissey, I'm sorry for the interruption. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I don't know if it -- if it interrupts or detracts from the question or not, but it's saved me asking it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you ever discuss with Bahrudin Fazlic this order?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time. The way I see it here, I never discussed this order because I had never seen it in this form until here. Whether I discussed his place and his role there, that's a question I could answer with a yes. I must have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, therefore, looking at that signature, what you can conclude is that in issuing that order, it's likely that Fazlic consulted with you before he did; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree. He did not consult me. That's for sure. There have been no consultations with me concerning this order, if he is indeed the one who signed it, and I cannot confirm that. Bahrudin Fazlic is alive. He lives in Sarajevo. If he can confirm that the signature is his, I have no choice but to agree. But I personally do not remember. He certainly didn't consult with me. But he is not at the end of the world. The two of us can be confronted. If he had indeed drafted this order, he could have written it following or looking at the current situation or looking at some prior order from above, such as from General Halilovic. If he had received such an order from General Halilovic, he could have written this order in keeping with that. But he certainly wasn't instructed by me to write it, and I didn't instruct him to do anything else, apart from what was strictly demanded by General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was going ask you this: Did you authorise him to conduct combat operations, as your deputy, in any written or oral order?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have authorised him to conduct combat operations in my name because I wasn't involved in that combat operations, but he was empowered by me to do -- to take whatever step is necessary to continue efficiently the combat operations if I wasn't around. However, I couldn't have conveyed or transferred to him the powers that I myself did not have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the break between the last lot of questioning and this one, have you had the opportunity to think of where you actually were on that day, the 11th?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the break was too short. Even if I had tried, I could not have remembered during the break where exactly I was on the 11th. I cannot remember with any certainty; although, I must say I didn't even try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final question about this document is this: Do you see any reference -- well, I have a preliminary final question first. Do you remember back in Zejnilagic -- the Zejnilagic order - I won't put it up on the screen now - but you might recall Zejnilagic mentioned two orders. He mentioned one from the chief of the Chief of Staff; he mentioned one from the 6th Corps. Do you recall that that was part of the preamble? Is that right? I'll --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The fact that there was no number attaching to the Chief of Staff's order indicates the likelihood that it was an oral order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no number; that's true. But he could have referred to the time when he received that order. There must be some sort of number. If there is no number whatsoever, I wouldn't know the reason, and we would probably never find out because Mr. Zejnilagic has moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he's moved, where is he now?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he passed away actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He died. He didn't move. He died; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not insulting your faith and I would appreciate it if you didn't insult mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expressed the thing as we Muslims tend to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Well, if that's the case, you can accept my apologies. But I do want to raise another matter, Mr. Gusic: Is it your practice to represent yourself to be polite and caring about Sefer Halilovic and concerned about protocol matters, on the one hand, but, on the other hand, make a completely unsolicited attack on the character of Asim Dzambasovic when it suits your purpose? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not my position. I'm not attacking anyone; although, I hold in very high esteem General Halilovic. I am simply stating the facts and I have stated those same facts personally when I contacted with him last year on the 26th of March. I told him on that occasion that I don't want to come into contact with people who are telling untruths. I am trying to be well-mannered. I am only human. Sometimes I make mistakes. But I believe that after all is said and done, all that one leaves behind is good words and good deeds or, on the contrary, bad words and bad deeds. I hope that I will have something to leave -- something good to leave behind, at least as much as you can fit behind your smallest thumbnail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Gusic, one thing that the author of that order did not leave behind on that order was a reference to Sefer Halilovic; do you agree with that? And I'm talking now of the order of the 11th of the 9th, which we have just been discussing.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the order with those signatures?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there is no reference to Sefer Halilovic, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no reference to any order that he issued which -- upon which this order is based, is there, either oral or written?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there is no such reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are the questions concerning that area. I now wish to turn to some very brief questions concerning the investigation of the crimes. This is out of chronology, but, Mr. Gusic, you understand you've asserted on previous occasions that you had effectively no or no meaningful involvement in Operation Neretva 93. You've now answered my questions concerning those orders and documents. And now I've got some questions concerning the course of the investigation. Mr. Gusic, you, I suggest, were advised about the killings in Grabovica late in the day or in the evening of the 9th of September, that being the day, the morning of which the killings were continuing; do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot either agree or disagree. I have told you already I cannot confirm precisely the date when I was informed thereof. I told you it was my assistant commander for security who notified me. I cannot say on which day. I don't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- think it was the day after the killings, but it was very shortly, maybe a couple of days after the killings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... three days in the past or two to three days in the past. Now, when you say your chief of security, do you mean Mr. Nermin Eminovic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean Mr. Eminovic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean the chief of the security. I mean my assistant commander for security. He is from the security sector, Eminovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this person's name Zajko Sahirlic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zajko Sahirlic? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit -- Defence document D26b. I'll just give you the number. Okay. This is DD00.2618. Could I just explain in relation to this document that there has been a glitch -- an error in the scanning of the Bosnian version, so that when Mr. Gusic receives this on the screen, it will only have the first page of the Bosnian version and not the second page, and therefor in fairness to him he ought to be provided with a paper copy of the entire thing, which we have present in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we have a copy obviously for the Prosecutors. And while that's being distributed, might I inquire of court staff what the next MFI number is that we --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As far as that will be MFI153.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I would seek that that be notified as MFI153.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. While we've been talking, Mr. Gusic, have you had the opportunity to briefly look at that document?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I didn't read it, but I can see it's a report received by the sector of military security of the command of the 6th Corps from the 44th Mountain Brigade on the 9th of September. That's the date of the drafting. However, the time when this was drafted, I can't see. It is drafted - and I must say the document is one I'm seeing for the first time - I was unable to see it in its original format because it was addressed originally to the security sector. It must have been received by my assistant for security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nermin Eminovic. And that's probably one among various pieces of information he had at his disposal when he was notifying me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get to -- to what Eminovic told you in a minute. At least from this document, it's quite plain -- could you just explain to the court who Mr. Sahirlic is and who Mr. Kevric is, the names of which are to be found at the bottom of this.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two officers were assistant commanders, one for security and another for intelligence in the 44th Mountain Brigade. So assistant commanders to Enes Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what this document consists of is it's a report sent by relatively senior officers from the 44th Mountain Brigade to the SVB, this is the military security sector, of the 6th Corps on the 9th -- on the evening of the 9th - evening or night, it's not quite clear, the timing - but at least at some stage on the 9th of September, 1993. Is that correct? Is that -- is that what it is in form? And I'll come to the substance in a minute rather than --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into the substance of it. Does this document indicate this: "We have information that members of the Bosnian army staying in the location of Grabovica physically abused the residents of Croatian nationality. There are indications that several murders were committed and a part of the Croatian population set off towards Jablanica. Members of the Jablanica SJB" - public security station - "and VP," - military police - "visited the site, and we shall provide you with new information in more detail"? Now, you can see that information in the middle paragraph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, Mr. Gusic, that information that there was the potential of several murders to be committed had to be relayed to you personally, given its importance, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, there are indications here only. There is no confirmation at this stage that a crime had been committed. These are only indications. And even though they are only indications, I should have been made aware. However, I wasn't made aware of these indications. And when I received my first information, it was already to find out that a crime had definitely been committed. At this stage, my assistant already had some information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, okay. So the position is this: What you say is you should have been told but you weren't; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, yes, I should have been told. I should have known there were indications; although, let me reiterate, this information probably arrived and -- piecemeal. The pieces of information arrived in bits and pieces, so they were probably waiting to collect the entire story. But yes, they should have told me about the indications right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other thing I want you to note is that in -- in the first paragraph, that in the night between the 8th and 9th of September some 250 detainees from the Dretelj camp arrived in Jablanica. Now, did you -- I understand what you say about when you were told about this, but it's the fact, isn't it, you came to know in due course that Dretelj camp detainees passed through Grabovica that very night of the killings, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. The way you're putting it now, I don't think I had this information. I did know, however, that former camp detainees had arrived, but I really cannot be certain about the dates. I have no reason to doubt this document. If that's what it says, then this probably happened at the time the document was compiled. But I cannot say that I knew that at the same time as the document was compiled. There has to be a time gap. This kind of document needed at least half a day to arrive from Jablanica if it was sent immediately. If it was waiting for a courier, it might arrive a day later. If it was transmitted in the original form, in the hard copy. If it was sent electronically, then of course it would travel much faster. But again, it was not addressed to me directly and it is not marked "urgent," so perhaps I was not informed of it right away. However, information that camp detainees had arrived in Jablanica did reach me, and it was the duty of the civilian authorities to accommodate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Gusic, I want to -- there's a lot of evidence in this case to be led through other witnesses concerning the investigation by military security of both of the crimes, at Grabovica and the -- at Uzdol as well. I'm not going to put those documents all to you, but I want to put to you a couple of general propositions and possibly two documents, just depending on what you say. But you know as a fact that your chief of -- your chief of military security, Nermin Eminovic, did assume the competence to investigate the killings at Grabovica and subsequently the killings at Uzdol. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I have heard that he took over the obligation to investigate the killings. I never knew it was his duty to carry out the investigation. I don't want to comment on this. He is alive, living in Sarajevo, and he can probably say more about it. My personal opinion is that he was not competent to do this on his own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if I may join company with you once again, briefly, Mr. Gusic. We agree with you, and we're not putting to you that he alone had the competence to do it. What we're putting to you is that he, in partnership with Namik Dzankovic, who was another military security operative, both of them answering to Jusuf Jasarevic, who was the chief of -- of military security in -- in Sarajevo, assumed the competence to investigate the -- both the offences, Grabovica initially and Uzdol subsequently. Now, do you agree that the SVB, the military security, assumed that competence?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any documents that would enable me to confirm this with certainty; however, I have no reason to doubt the documents you have and I am not challenging what General Jasarevic stated or the other persons you have mentioned. You probably have reason to believe that they did, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, could the witness please be -- now, just excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, just excuse me a moment. I just want to verify something before I put a document to you. Mr. Gusic, could -- let me just ask you this: Did you ever see any of the correspondence that passed between your chief of security, Nermin Eminovic, on the one hand, and Jusuf Jasarevic in Sarajevo, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents Eminovic showed in their original form are documents I could have seen. I could have seen them if he showed them to me. But there was no reason for me to see most of the documents because, as I said, the correspondence went along the security chain of command, so I didn't see a large part of them. However, there is a part that I did see and, if I saw them, I would note this down in some way or mark it in some way, either by my signature or by writing down the name of the person who told me about this document. When I saw a document like that, I left a written trace on the document itself to show that I had seen it, because these were always strictly confidential documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, could the witness please be shown now Exhibit -- Defence document D472, which is DD00.2178. And it's MFI154.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a direction --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an instruction to my assistant -- or rather, the chief, Nermin Eminovic. It was probably sent electronically to the attention of Zajko Sihirlic, the assistant for security in the 44th Brigade. And as I can now see the heading of the corps command, you can see what I said. The bit that's meeting in the previous command, I want says: "The Bosnia and Herzegovina, Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, commander of the 6th Corps," so it was standard when the 6th Corps was issuing documents to have this heading and then it would be evident that this was a document issued by the core command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But just in terms of this document, is there a marking here on this document indicating that you saw it.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on this document. No, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just let me ask you some questions about the substance of the document anyway. This is a direction from the -- the chief of military security at the 6th Corps, Nermin Eminovic, to Mr. Sihirlic, who as we understand it is down at the 44th Brigade, to take all necessary measures to shed light on the massacre of Croatian civilians in Dreznica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dreznica is the region in which Grabovica is to be found; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe this was being viewed as a whole region. In that context, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dreznica is a separate village, but the term could also be used to cover the broader territory around Dreznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Well, what I want to know is: Did you know and did you agree with Eminovic giving this direction?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this. And let me tell you again: There was no reason for me to know. This could have been ordered by the security administration in Sarajevo, that is, General Jasarevic, telling him to cooperate with the other corps because Dreznica was not in the area of responsibility of our corps but they were asking for help, and if he had the approval of General Jasarevic, then he could undertake this kind of activity even without my knowledge. Because I'm not trying to say that the commander was not allowed to know. It wasn't all that secret. But if General Jasarevic wanted to involve as few people as possible in this investigation and keep the information in as narrow a circle as possible about the crime, then he could have reduced this to the smallest possible number of people to be involved, and this was probably done with a view to discovering the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Gusic, you had to be told about this because if there was to be an investigation, it might involve the use of your military police, mightn't it? So you had to be told because it would impact upon your use of military police or it could impact upon your use of military police. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to be told, because for this kind of work my assistant for security could use the police battalion and this would fall within his competence. He had authority to do that, and he could give the military police battalion commander the order to do that, or any military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. -- Mr. Gusic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he could give that order. But you were able to use the military police for your own pushes. And what I'm putting to you to: You had informed that the military police might be deployed in this way for your own purposes; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should have been told that because if I was planning to use the military police battalion in combat operations, which would be exclusively within my sphere of competence, then I would have to be informed that the unit was deployed doing this work and that I couldn't count on it. However, at that point in time, I had defined the forces I was using and my assistant knew that, so I don't wish to go into what his intentions and decisions were at the time. What I can assert is that I did not know they were deployed in that way, and this is the first time I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, what I'm putting to you is that you very well knew, regardless of what your military security representative was compelled to tell you -- what I'm putting to you is you very well knew that he was actively pursuing the investigation into the crime at Grabovica and ultimately the crime at Uzdol. Now, do you agree that you knew that or do you say you didn't know that he was doing that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know he was doing that, but I did know that information was coming through him because he told me what had happened down there, so he had that information. But I didn't know about his role in these activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, you've said in the past that you got the news about the Uzdol massacre on the radio. Do you stand by that account?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the media. I think it was first on the radio, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I cut you off there, but could we please show the witness D67, that is, DD00.0261, and it's to be MFI155. Now, have you got that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got that? Now, here's a letter written by you to the commander of the 3rd Corps - is that correct - on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I probably wrote it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But please, I cannot confirm with absolute certainty that I wrote this document. Today I can agree that this is the information I had. And when I heard about this information, I checked with the commander and on the basis of the information I had received from Buza, I do not deny that I could have written something like this. However, as this is correspondence between commanders, I cannot say with any certainty whether and when I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you note that it's dated the 16th of September, 1993. And, second of all, you note that you've had a report, an official operative report, from Mr. Buza. Does that assist you to put a date on it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't assist me. I say again that I did not see that report until you showed it to me here. I received information from Buza in a completely different form. It was much shorter, more meagre. It referred to the losses and the casualties in the village of Uzdol. I did not see the entire report before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Because looking at that document there, you've got no reason to doubt that you did send that document, have you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information here is in accordance with the information I received, and I do not deny that I might have written this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my information indicated that this was ideological propaganda activity fabricated by the HVO because that's what I had heard from the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. But -- and I'm not being critical of you in any way, Mr. Gusic. I just want you to be clear. You don't dispute the authenticity of that document, and what you say is it's highly likely you did send it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the authenticity of the document but, rather, about the authenticity of the information contained in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not challenging the authenticity of the information contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's okay. But you're not challenging the authenticity of the document either, are you, Mr. Gusic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And I want to put this to you: That document isn't signed by you, is it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't recall. Don't ask me that. But I don't see my signature on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right, Mr. Gusic. Now, it's the fact, isn't it, that your -- Mr. Eminovic, once the Uzdol investigation became -- once Uzdol was -- had happened, Mr. Eminovic engaged himself in the investigation of -- as part of the SVB, engaged himself in the investigation. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation? From what you showed me, yes. That's what you say. Yes. But at the time, I didn't know that he was participating in the investigation as actively as these documents show.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, I want to ask you a question very quickly about the military police. There was in Konjic one company of military police and there was in Jablanica another company of military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when -- if those units were in a -- a properly upkept army and properly resourced and kept up to -- up to the requisite level of manpower, those units would have had in them each approximately 70 men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on the structure of the unit and its purpose. A police company could be bigger than that number. But this was the minimum number it had to have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these units, in fact, had less than the full complement of men in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes. I think there is a report on manpower levels and from it you can see that they were not up to the requisite manpower levels because this kind of unit requires men who are properly trained for military police tasks. They have to be trained differently from other men. They have certain tasks and obligations that are essentially different from those executed by other soldiers in other units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, in terms of military police numbers, there was also a -- a smaller platoon of military police attaching to the 44th Brigade itself in Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can check that in the establishment, but I think that's so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Very well. Now, it's also the fact isn't it, now -- that's the end of that line of questioning. And I now want to turn to some other information concerning your activities at that time. You're familiar with the logbook -- the logbooks of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I familiar with the logbook?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with part of the logbooks, the ones I kept. But as for all the records and all the logbooks, there was a special logbook that was kept by the security organ which I can't say I'm fully familiar with. The operations organ also had a logbook. I think I am familiar with the operations part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you shown a copy of any logbook in recent times?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to see only a war diary of the 44th Brigade, but not of the 6th Corps, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown D334, which is MFI156. While that's being -- sorry, which is DD00.1544, and it will be Marked for Exhibit 156. And I believe I neglected to offer for tender the previous three exhibits, and I offer those for tender.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the front page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could the next page please --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does that appear to be?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the cover page of a logbook, an operative or operations logbook of the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it says underneath. There seems to be something covered up. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could we show the witness the next page, please. Very well. We need to show the page after that. I'm sorry. No, we'll have to keep going, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the second page now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could we just go to -- I think it's the third page, where the -- the entries begin. Very well.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third page is a record of events, and it lists the reports that arrived and the time when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Now, looking at that -- at that document. Is it apparent -- I'm going to take you to the 8th of September --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Can I enquire of the Court. Does the Court and the Prosecutor have before them an English translation or -- oh, good. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, Mr. Gusic. Very well. Do you see there that there are -- this is dated the 8th of September, 1993? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at 1150 hours is there a regular combat report from the 44th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1150 hours.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11.50, combat report from the 44th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see at 1330 hours there are many different reports that come in but one of them is a regular report from the 45th Brigade? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see at 1957 hours there's a regular combat report from the 45th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time? 11 ...?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19.57, daily combat report, yes, 45th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and at 2040 hours there's a regular combat report from the 44th Brigade. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20.40, daily combat report, yes. 44th, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you also -- and now we'll need to, I think, turn over the page now and go to 0800 hours on the 9th of September. Now, I just want to ask you about one there, and not to misrepresent the position. There's a combat report from the 6th Corps to the supreme corps -- to the Sjever [phoen] SVK, which is the General Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is 0800 hours.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 0800 hours? Yes. The time isn't stated. It says: "Combat report between 08.00 and 13.10. In the interval between 0800 and 1310, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have at 13.10 a regular combat report by the 45th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there's a combat report from the 44th; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then at last you have one from Sefer Halilovic which is mentioned immediately below that.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Jablanica IKM?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's an example of the IKM word being used.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then here you have an order for technical and materiel equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you keep going down, you've got further combat reports at 2100 hours from the 45th Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 45th Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you've got another combat report sent by you -- or by the 6th Corps to the General Staff at 2340 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then if you'd turn over -- now we have -- just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we turn over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have -- this is on the 12th of September. Do you see the entries under the 12th of September?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th of September, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Can you see there at the -- it's the second entry. It doesn't have a time, but it's a regular combat report from the Neretvica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's -- that's the 45th Brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see what brigade it is. Regular combat report, but what brigade. Neretvica BB, that's battalion. Probably it's the 45th, but I can't really see it all that well on this document. I think it says "Neretvica."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "BB." I don't know. But certainly it says "Neretvica." That implies other the brigade or a part of the brigade, the 45th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And do you notice there at -- at a time after 1520 hours there's another report from the 44th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1500 hours?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the time after 1520 hours. You'll see it's three down -- it's three entries down from that.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the 45th Brigade here. The 43rd, the 9th, the 43rd. I don't see the report from the 45th. What time was it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you see a time entry, 1520 hours, which relates to a regular combat report of the 43rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you count two lines, two down from that.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 44th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Now, Mr. Gusic -- well, you confirm that that is a document of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably is. It probably is. This is the operations logbook of the operations and training organ, who was keeping a record of the incoming and outgoing mail. The title "Operations logbook," is a bit misleading. It's not really the right title to indicate the contents, but this is certainly a record of incoming and outgoing mail and information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well,

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I offer that for tender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I want to put a conclusion to you, Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of the orders issued, because of the correspondence that's been tendered or being offered for tender, because of your constant contacts with combat units, and because of your corps' involvement in the investigation, I put it to you that you were deeply involved in Neretva 93 and I further put it to you so that you understand where this question is going that you have deliberately attempted to minimise your involvement in that operation. Do you agree with either or both of those propositions?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with either of them. My participation in Operation Neretva -- and it seems I have to keep repeating. I didn't know the name of the operation. I knew that combat operations were going on, and my only obligation -- the only obligation of the corps command was to put certain units at the disposal of the IKM in Jablanica, where General Halilovic was in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The last series of questions I have before this cross-examination finishes is a -- is a chronological series. And where we departed from the strict chronology -- chronology earlier and plunged into these orders was at the date of the 5th of September; namely, the meeting of Dobro Polje. On the 5th of September, I put it to you that Sefer Halilovic left Dobro Polje suddenly and went back to Sarajevo. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but it's probably true. If you say so, I have no reason to doubt your words, or the general's, if he says it is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also know that -- that at that -- on the 6th of September, Bakir Alispahic arrived in the region of Jablanica? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying again I don't know the date, but sometime around that time, the period that we are discussing, Minister Alispahic did go down there. Yes, that's -- that much I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, although the Prosecutor has asked you to examine a number of orders by General Arif, as you -- I shouldn't say "general" -- by Arif Pasalic in the period between the 4th and the 7th of September, you didn't see any of those documents at the time, did you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them for the first time when they were shown to me here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On the 8th of September, there was a meeting -- well, the evidence may show that there was a meeting at Donja Jablanica between various commanders involved in the Operation Neretva 93 at the base of Zulfikar Alispago. And my question to you is: On the 8th of September, did you attend a meeting at the base of Zulfikar Alispago concerning the operations -- the offensive operations in the Neretva Valley?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your deputy, Fazlic, attend?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think he did. But I don't know for sure. Bahrudin Fazlic is available, and he must know the facts better than I do. I cannot confirm about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 8th of September, did you find yourself that evening in Konjic -- well, no, I withdraw that question. I'm going to put another one to you. I suggest to you that on the 8th of September -- the night of the 8th of September, that in fact Sefer Halilovic along with some other persons, including Seli [phoen] Halilovic and his driver and a variety of other people, some of whom I'll name in a minute, were present in Konjic, where you also were? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be specific about the dates, but I did meet a couple of times; I can even say several times with General Halilovic in the ARK building. That much is true. But what other people attended in addition to the general, I cannot specify with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know a man -- did you meet a man called Kerim Lucarevic on that occasion, a man who had been a leader of military police in Sarajevo and was at this time forming a political party? Perhaps to assist your memory, a man with the nickname of "Doktor"?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the doctor. I know him personally. It's no problem to identify him. But as far as I remember, I did not meet with him in the area of Jablanica, in the area of the zone of responsibility of the 6th Corps, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I want to take you to the next day, the 9th of September, and ask you this: That -- do you know a man called Ibro Puric?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibro Puric, certainly. I know him. He was the commander of the reconnaissance and sabotage brigade that at the time became an integral part of the 6th Corps. Before that, it used to be part of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, I'll just ask you about what was happening on the 9th now. I put to you that Ibro Puric was present in Konjic on that-- on the night of the 8th and 9th and was present in -- in Konjic on that day of the 9th when the news came through to your headquarters that there might have been killings in Grabovica. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Ibro Puric was. He's still alive. He lives in Zenica. And he could have even written it down or maybe he remembers it better. I am certainly not well placed to remember where Ibro Puric was at the time. The only thing I can say is that he was supposed to be together with his unit and his unit was supposed to be deployed at Kitcevo [phoen] village -- in Bjelinici village, rather. That's where his unit was. Whether he was around in Konjic in that period, I can neither confirm nor deny.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you've already given an account of what -- of how you heard about Grabovica. I want to go to the 12th of September. Have you ever been shown an order from Commander Delic that is supposed to be directed to you and to Sefer Halilovic concerning, first of all, the scope of Operation Neretva 93 and, secondly, the need to investigate certain crimes? Have you ever been shown such a document?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the Prosecutor who showed me that document, if we mean the same document, the one where my Chief of Staff notifies the commander of the information on the basis of which this order is written. If that's the document you mean, I saw it in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Just excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is a document, OTP 65 ter number is 57, and its ERN number is 01805265, and it will become MFI157. Mr. Gusic, what I'm trying to do is get a copy of that document up on the screen here, and then I'll ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well,-- thanks. All right. Now, does that document record that the Chief of Staff of the 6th Corps has given Delic certain information?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you send that to the Chief of Staff, to give Delic that information?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. And I must say this was not the usual practice. It was not the usual practice for an underling to comment on their superior's decision, so my --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Chief of Staff violated the procedure here. I did not send him to the commander to say that, nor did he have my approval for doing so. And if you want my opinion, he shouldn't have said anything to the commander because the commander should have ex officio received all that information directly from General Halilovic or from some other person who was together with General Halilovic. Dzevad Tirak, my Chief of Staff, in other words, should not have conveyed this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because -- if you'd just stop there just for one moment.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was outside the regular procedural channels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you agree that if the regular procedural channels apply, then this order here looks very much like you are the one who's reported directly to Delic about what happened. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It says quite clearly here: "Chief of Staff of the 6th Corps informed me of the decision of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command." My name is not mentioned in any of these lines, nor is any reference made to me personally. My Chief of Staff was Tirak Dzevad. And he did what he did, and I continue to think to this day that it was not proper for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is extremely hypocritical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, your position about this order, in any event, is that you didn't receive it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I could not identify it the very moment when I see it, but I did eventually receive it because it has something to do with my Chief of Staff, so it must have been sent to me, among other people, if for no other reason, than to let me know that the basis for this order was information provided by my Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But -- and just in terms of the timing of that document, are you able to say looking at it that it arrived at Jablanica at 1414 hours?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just look through the whole document. All I can see now is para 1 and 3. If you could downsize it a little, zoom out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he arrived at 1414 hours on the 12th of September, 1993. "Sent to Prozor at 20.30."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gusic, this isn't your problem, but it's going to arise in relation to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, you don't have that in front of you. The witness is looking at the -- at the document, and where on the English version it says: "Stamp," is actually a relatively advanced stamp. Could I ask, therefore that, the screen show for all parties the Bosnian original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, would you just bear with me for a moment, please. I want to show the Judges that -- the timing there, and the Prosecution, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. So having regard to -- to the timing on this document, it appears to arrive at Jablanica on 14 minutes past 2.00 in the afternoon, 1414 hours, and it appears to be sent off to Prozor at 2030 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can read this on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just -- again, Mr. Gusic, just bear with me for one second?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the English version come back up, for those who normally use English. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just having regard to that order, it's evident that the order itself concerns, among other things, the -- what is described as -- I'll just take you to the first paragraph or the preamble. It says -- it is regarding planned combat operations towards Prozor and Mostar. Now, do you agree that that's what's specified in the preamble?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that there's an order to re-examine the decision and the decision being the decision to pursue the attack in those directions? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the activities related to attack but also all the other activities. It says: "Review the decision in all its aspects," and the decision is made up of several elements: "Engagement of forces, manoeuvre, axes of action, combat disposition or deployment, depending on the level, and combat readiness." All these elements should be reviewed under this decision. The entire decision is being questioned, supervised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. But there's also, isn't there, a requirement that the -- the Grabovica incident be investigated? Or at least for the information --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- for the information to be checked. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is said that the information should be reviewed, verified, and if irregularities are found, perpetrators should be identified and punished, and everything should be done to prevent a further occurrence of similar incidents. It says: "Order the commander of the -- or rather, the deputy commander of the 9th Brigade and the 1st Corps to immediately return to Sarajevo to solve problems within the unit."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gusic, if Sefer Halilovic was the commander in his own right of that -- of that operation, I put to you there was absolutely no need to address this document to you personally and that, rather, addressing it in that way makes it quite clear that Commander Delic regarded you as a part of the chain of command in this operation. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with you. General Halilovic commanded the forces on the ground involved in the operation we are talking about, and the reason why I received this document is probably only one; namely, that the source of information was, as it turns out, my Chief of Staff. That's the only reason why it was sent to me. I didn't even have to receive it necessarily in its original form. It could have been sent to me in some other format. It was a way of asking me to -- of asking me whether the information provided by my Chief of Staff was correct. This commander should try to achieve both objectives by writing one single paper. But the whole thing shouldn't have happened in the first place, even though the commander did not agree with the decision. So it is not a typical piece of correspondence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gusic, on the 13th -- or you've indicated you don't know the dates of the attack at Uzdol, but what I want to put to you is this: That after the Uzdol attack -- and I want to ask you whether you were told about this -- after the Uzdol attack had taken place and failed, there was an angry meeting of the commanders at which Zejnilagic and Hakanovic and other local commanders became very angry with Enver Buza because he failed to comply with the attack direction. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not attend the meeting. I don't even know whether it was actually held. It probably was. I'm not doubting your words as such for a moment, but I'm not aware of the atmosphere among the commanders because I -- or their feelings, because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I might assist your memory with this. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown document D22a. Now, this is DD00.0076, and it will be MFI158.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the English version of this document, Mr. Gusic, it simply records that there is a signature on the bottom. It says: "For the Chief of General Staff, Sefer Halilovic," and then it's got the words "a signature" underneath it. You looking at that document are able to say that that signature underneath there is quite plainly the signature of Vehbija Karic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a look?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought you had it. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And perhaps if the -- if the B/C/S version could be displayed to the Judges and to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the signature I see here does not belong to General Halilovic. At least, I don't think it does; although, I'm not an expert and I cannot be emphatic, but it doesn't look like General Halilovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks to me like the signature of the brigadier commander, Vehbija Karic. I'm reading: "V" -- letter "V" and then "Karic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can identify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although, I don't remember his -- Karic's signature specifically, so I can't confirm it, but I can read "V." Karic in this handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the English version go back to the English speakers now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I suggest -- what I'm putting to you now is that document that's signed by Karic appears to be a combat document. And indeed --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Moreover, it's a combat document assigning a task or a mission and appointing the commander for that axis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now,-- and quite plainly -- and in fact we -- well, we'll come to another document now, but what I want to put to you is that this is quite plainly Mr. Halilovic issuing an order. This document here being Karic, but the next one which you'll look at will clench the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown D22, which is already in evidence and is marked for Exhibit 124 -- MFI124.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see this. It looks to me like another order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first blush. I haven't read the contents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. I'll give you a chance to read it. Just, first of all, could you just notice the date on it. And is the date of this one like the previous one, the 15th?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th and the -- I didn't look at the date at the previous document, but this is the -- from the 15th of September, 1993. A strictly confidential number, 21-1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to -- I'm going to have to ask you to look at the date of the previous one. I'll do that in a minute. But take it from me -- assume for a moment that the date of the previous one was the same. What you have then --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that. I have no reason to disbelieve it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand that. You have a document therefore that's signed by Karic on behalf of Sefer Halilovic that's dated the 15th of -- of September, which is a combat document without any doubt at all. And then after that you have a similar document with a couple of terminology changes but similar in all other essences, which is signed personally by Sefer Halilovic on the 15th of September as well; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that. I can see that on the screen as we speak. A document signed by General Halilovic. And moment ago I saw a very similar document signed by Brigadier Karic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I want to put to you is this: That the Karic document, D22a -- sorry, MFI158, and the Halilovic document, which is MFI124, are both orders that fall within that part of the inspection team order, the power to solve problems that arise, and the inspection team order being the order from the 30th of August, and that in particular these orders arose from the crisis caused -- and the argument caused by Buza's failure which occurred between the leaders in the afternoon and evening of the 14th of September. Now, bearing in mind I understand your difficulty with dates, but do you agree that that's the basis on which both Karic and ultimately Halilovic produced those two orders?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree that these are orders issued by the inspection team. Those are orders governing combat operations. But I'm not saying, mind you, that they do not follow from the orders issued earlier by the inspection team. You can see the link with paragraph 3, where it speaks of radical changes. But this is beyond the realm of inspection work. This is at the level of command and control. I don't know about this other document. I believe it is the same. I believe both documents are firmly in the area of command and control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at all events, what you say is you don't know whether there was in fact a crisis such as the one I've described late on the 14th of the 9th where the -- where the other commanders criticised Mr. Buza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I was not aware of that, because I wasn't directly in charge of those combat activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I understand that. Now, Mr. Gusic --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one -- all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me press on because of the time factor. Mr. Gusic, did you receive a request from the deputy commander of the entire Bosnian army, Stjepan Siber, to inform you what the situation -- to -- sorry, to inform him about the rumours concerning killings at Uzdol on the 16th of September?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether that request came from the commander or the commander's deputy, but there were several requests of that nature and all of them were relying on the information received from Enver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, yesterday you promised me that you could finish your cross-examination in two hours. Now we have gone for three hours already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, Your Honour can see the situation that obtains, and can I indicate this -- because as I've said, this witness is one who's not to be cut off because he's being asked for explanations and it's not his fault. I don't criticise him for it. He has given some lengthy answers, as you've seen. It's not his fault. But the number of questions I've asked have been, in any event, relatively confined. But, however, can I indicate what is left. I've got a number of chronology questions which cover the period the 16th of the 9th, which we're now at, and three documents, and that will then will followed by some odds and ends questions, frankly, to clean up, and that's the end. So we are very nearly at the end now. I do appreciate I've gone over time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So how much time do you estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think 15 minutes for the thing I'm on now, and then I would -- I would very much appreciate a short break -- I know we haven't had one, because collecting your thoughts can save time as well frankly. There may be some matters that I've got here that I may not need to ask, and I just want to consider those, if I may. I think that would be time well spent, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I hope you could leave some time for the redirect as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- as Judges questions at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And by the way, we have a lot of documents to tender, so I would like to ask you or your team to submit to me a new list of the documents with the MFI numbers on it so -- like the Prosecution did in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, as the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's high time to take a break because, you know, we have been sitting here for 90 minutes, and we have to take a break for 20 minutes, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We have saved time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, just before I ask you the last series of questions in the chronology, I have a question for you. On Thursday prior to giving your evidence, prior to being called by the Prosecution to give your evidence, and in the -- in the two hours before you gave that evidence, did you receive a visit from any person from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to coming to The Hague, did you meet with an individual by the name of Mr. Dugalic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown D122, please. That is DD00 -- sorry, DD00.0524, and it should be marked as MFI159.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excellent. Now, is this document a document signed by Stjepan Siber inquiring --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that -- is that addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's addressed to the corps command. It could have been received -- as it's information having the character of information and propaganda, it could have been received by the assistant for morale, the assistant for security, the assistant for security, my deputy, the Chief of Staff, or myself. This is a general document. I should have been informed about it. I needn't have received it personally, but I should have been informed about it, and I think that I did have this information and that this information was requested on several occasions, both by the commander and by General Siber and perhaps by some other officers and commanders in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And -- very well. Thank you. And do you note also the nature of the -- of the signature -- sorry, the nature of the signature there that Siber signs explicitly as "deputy"? Do you agree? And uses the form we discussed earlier?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that does not have the form of a document issued by the deputy. It is a document having the form of a document issued by the commander. So he was actually signing for the commander at that point. He was acting on the commander's behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I offer that document. Could the witness please be shown a document -- Defence document 23. This has the number DD00.0080 and it will be MFI160.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document that's about to come up on the screen is a document concerning cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have the front page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Does it indicate that it's sent from Sarajevo on the 16th of September?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates that it was compiled in Sarajevo on the 16th of September, 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it indicate that no later than -- in paragraph 1, does it indicate that the latest at which combat operations can cease is 1200 hours on the 18th of September?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And does it indicate in fact that there was already a cease-fire agreement dated the 30th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- very well. Now --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "an agreement." It doesn't say "cease-fire," but an agreement which probably contained provisions about a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. I won't press you about that, Mr. Gusic. What I want you to do is look at the second paragraph, if you don't mind, and consider the -- one might say the caveats or exceptions from this order. Paragraph 2: "Units of -- units of the Bosnian army are allowed to act only in the event of" -- and then the order goes on to explain some of the events.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "A breach by the HVO or joint forces." Now, can I ask you this -- well, perhaps we'll go on a bit further: "In other words, operations are allowed only in when unit positions and lives of the members of the BiH army are threatened including the territories and facilities under their control. Or" -- and this is the bit I stress --"or if civilian population living in BiH army-controlled territories comes under threat from the HVO or joint forces. Now, let me ask you this: As far as you know, did the population of Mostar stop being under threat from the HVO forces at this time?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I Cannot assert this with any certainty, but according to information coming from the command of the 4th Corps, the threat never ceased in that period. There was always activity on the side where members of the Army of BH were. Whether there were provocations from the other side, I cannot say. But according to information coming from the corps command, Mostar was constantly under threat in that period. That's the information that reached me. There may have been other information. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. And would you be prepared to assert that the HVO loyally and honestly stuck to that cease-fire agreement when it was entered into?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that with respect to the 4th Corps which was part of the ABiH, let alone the HVO. I wasn't a member of the HVO, so I don't know.
