utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody from the HVO might know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask the question another way: On the 17th and 18th of September, did the HVO soldiers stop shooting at your soldiers and did they stop shelling and did they stop holding prisoners in camps and did they stop blockading Mostar and generally behaving as you'd found them to behave over the previous months?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they did. I think their behaviour continued as it had been. The intensity of their activity might have dropped in some parts, but I don't think their activity ceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic the final chronology questions are these: You've already been asked questions -- I withdraw those. I've covered those. That's the end of the chronology questions. And I now have one technical area to ask you about that will be very short indeed. I undertake to all parties in court, but it's a relevant matter. You're aware of a military formation entitled "an operations group," which is a temporary military formation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you had an involvement in an operations group yourself on Igman at one stage.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The rules relating to -- operations groups are effectively an ad hoc group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it an ad hoc group. It's a temporary formation formed to carry out a specific task, and on completion of that task or the abandonment of that task, those formations are generally disbanded and restored to their organic composition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, as you understand -- the -- the nature of each different operations group depends upon the tasks and powers given to it in the order which creates it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in order to assist the -- if you like, the ambit of authority of the commander of a particular operations group, you have to look at the order creating that group; is that correct??

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a procedure that would indicate the easiest way to conduct correspondence and assistance; although, it could be done differently, through instructions, guidelines, or a number of other documents. However, most frequently and the easiest way to do it is through orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, in the past and, in fact, on the 16th and 17th of November in the year 2000, when you made a statement to the ICTY investigators, you said this - and I'm just going to ask you whether it's accurate or not - "The duties and responsibilities of the operations group commander" - it's at page 4 of that document - "The duties and responsibilities of the operations group commander were written in each particular order by which each operations group was formed. However, everyone understood that the commander had less authority than a corps commander but that he had more authority than a brigade commander." Now, I've read two -- two sentences to you there. But is that true?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. The brigade commander did not have to be part of the operations group. A lower-ranking customer of a smaller unit might be that. So the level would not be important whether it's a company or a brigade. In the case we are discussing, in the case of Igman, they were brigades. So he would have more authority than a brigade commander and less than the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You never saw any order indicating that an operations group had been set up under the command of Sefer Halilovic for the purpose of Neretva 93, did you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, an operations group is a rather smaller group than the assembly of troops that were used in Operation Neretva 93; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operations group is a smaller group? Well, that's a moot point. I wouldn't agree with that. It's a temporary formation, and its size depends on the specific task at hand. The operations group can be bigger or smaller, depending on the units that form part of that operations group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I want to ask you some final -- some final questions about the order that would create an operations group. First of all, in order to appoint Sefer Halilovic to head an operations group, there would have to have been an order of the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should have been, according to the correct procedure, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the order appointing Sefer Halilovic --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the competence to appoint commanders belonged only to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you say "appoint commanders," just to be clear, you're referring to higher-level commanders, are you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. And in the order creating an operations group, it would be necessary to spell out to whom that operations group was subordinated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. Unless it was formed by a commander using only his troops. If it was formed by a corps commander, then it would be something logical. However, if it's composed of several different kinds of units, then that would be true, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, because an operations group is a temporary group, it's necessary in the order creating the operations group to spell out either what those units are or how those units are to be brought into the operations group in the future; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would facilitate the work of the command of the operations group. Certainly. I don't want to comment on the appearance of each document because it would depend on the ability of the person drawing up the document, but that's what it should specify, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And finally, the commander of an operations group would not have power on his own to unilaterally resubordinate units from other corps into his operations group unless he was specifically authorised to do that in the order that he had; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's logical, yes. He could not have power to use any other units without approval, the approval of his superior. So only his superior could give him that approval. And, for example, I could not give approval for the use of units from the 3rd Corps; only the army commander could do that; only General Delic could have given such authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gusic, thank you for your considerable patience. Those are the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Morrissey. Any redirect, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Re-examined by Ms. Chana:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll start with this last point straightaway. Mr. Gusic, you said that Commander Delic would have the authority to give Sefer Halilovic -- to resubordinate units. Delic could -- could authorise Halilovic to resubordinate certain units to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't have to authorise it. He could order him. The commander issues orders. The commander could put those units at his disposal. The commander could order me or the commander of some other corps to put certain units at the disposal of General Halilovic. That would not have the form of approval but of an order. He could also authorise General Halilovic to do that himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he could authorise Sefer Halilovic to resubordinate units the way he wanted, according to his own discretion.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could. Yes. He could, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from some of the documents I showed you in my direct examination, was that the case, that Sefer Halilovic did indeed resubordinate these units to his IKM command?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Some of the documents, I don't recall whether you showed them all to me in the courtroom, but during the proofing you showed me documents where this was the case. I think this was the case with the units entitled "Handzar Divizija," which were part of the Zulfikar Detachment. I don't know whether I saw the documents here in the courtroom but I did see it during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I did show you some documents, and I don't want to waste the Court's time, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise an objection here? It's very desirable that, first of all, the Defence knows what documents are being put to the witness for the purpose of him giving an opinion and, secondly, it's very desirable that it be made sure that they are documents that are in evidence, because otherwise they are hard to test. Now, the line of questioning is perfectly legitimate, but it just better be made clear exactly which documents are being relied on, and if they're not in-court documents, then they shouldn't be relied on, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could ask the witness to answer the question first. And if you still have some doubts on it, you may raise it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, I can expand on my answer. There were units from the 1st Corps, and I saw that document - I think it was shown in the courtroom - where I was duty-bound to receive them at Bradina and help them to proceed through Jablanica. This is a document which shows that General Halilovic was competent to use units from the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Zulfikar Unit? Was that resubordinated by an order of Sefer Halilovic that you did see in this court?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you could show each document again but it's just covering old territory, and I'm mindful of the time and the fact that the Court would like to put some questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was an order in which the late Arif Pasalic, General Pasalic, puts the Zulfikar Unit at the disposal of the IKM and General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Gusic, it's been put to you that normally an order is required when an operational group is set up so that all the duties and what the commander can do and -- are written in detail in that particular order. Is that -- that's what you have stated to learned counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the procedure that should be respected; however, in practice there were other kinds of activities. Something could be done orally, for example, and then a written order would arrive later on or only an oral order would be issued. However, I beg not to have to comment on the orders or instructions issued by my superiors. It's up to them to tell you why they did things in certain ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite right, Mr. Gusic. It's for your superiors to know why they do. But you would confirm that there were occasions that oral -- oral orders could be given?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did happen, yes. It did happen. There were very many such instances. More than one, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- could it also be the case, Mr. Gusic, that a -- a written document, a written order, would be given giving a kind of a largesse theme but the more detailed aspects of it would come out during discussions and during oral -- and an oral order after that as to the -- as to the fullness of the implementation of any particular operation or task?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just described is the best method of arriving at the best solution. The commanders, whenever they had the opportunity, would ask us for our opinion, and then we would discuss our joint proposals, and this would be transformed into an order on the spot. That was the best method and it was used wherever practicable, because after all, it was the commander in the field who was best familiar with the situation in the field, and Commander Delic appreciated that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gusic. These were difficult times for the army, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was a lot to be done.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were times perhaps the administration could not keep up with the -- the -- what was actually happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for other commands, but I know that very frequently my command and I had to do things orally. And whether everything was covered by orders or not, I don't know. The situation would change from hour to hour sometimes, and there were a lot of oral orders issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will take you to this 30th August document. Do you need to see it or do you remember it? That's the one which set up -- this is the one that we -- we've had this translation problem over.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it. Yes, I recall the document. I don't need to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that document. Would it have been possible for some oral discussions to have taken place in respect of that document as to the implementation of the -- the lines of attack in the Operation Neretva?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told Defence counsel that in paragraph 3, discussing drastic changes, this would lead to such a conclusion. However, whether this happened or not, I can't say. It does, however, provide for the possibility of discussing the axes, drawing up a plan, or continuing combat operations in -- with new plans. It does provide for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us again - and I know you have talked about this at some length, but nevertheless it would bear a bit of repeating - did this in fact, on the ground, did it -- what Sefer Halilovic was doing, did it translate into command authority for the operation?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that one can consider it to be so. I assert that he was the commander in the field for those combat operations and that he was the actual authority on the ground, the authority that was respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us why you know this. What were the indicia to -- for you to draw this particular conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I draw it from everything that happened on the ground. He could use the forces of the 6th Corps, of the 1st Corps. He issued a decision on a change in the plan. He was in charge of the operation. He led the troops. And he was able to assign any task that had to do with those combat operations. And this would constitute an order for all of us who were out there in the field, and I think that part of the documents you showed me indicate that, as well as the documents shown by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, to your awareness and knowledge, did the troops on the ground, did all the soldiers and the units, whatever, follow Sefer Halilovic's orders?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the soldiers -- the men carried out the orders, but I think that the commanders at all levels respected and complied with the orders. I'm not saying that they executed each and every one of them. It would depend on the circumstances. But I think that they did everything in their power to implement those orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did anybody, yourself included, ever challenge Mr. Halilovic's authority to give such orders and his authority in the area of operations, the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, never to this day have I challenged the authority or the significance of everything done by General Halilovic. I have a deep respect for it all. Nobody ever challenged it. Nobody ever dared challenge his contribution. I don't want to comment on the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not challenge his authority once, clearly, because you respected General Halilovic. Were there any other reasons why nobody challenged it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see a single reason why anyone should challenge his authority, nor do I know that anyone did challenge the authority of General Halilovic. I don't wish to say, however, that when there were discussions on certain issues, I necessarily agreed with General Halilovic's positions. This does not mean, however, that I challenged or brought into question in any way his importance. However, let me repeat: I have never in my life said things I thought the other side wanted to hear. I always said what my opinion was. I may have made mistakes, because I'm only human after all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gusic. You did say that you had several meetings with Sefer Halilovic during the course of mid-September, when all of this was happening. Did he ever suggest to you that he has no authority -- command authority whatsoever? Did -- were are there any utterances made to you saying to you that, "Look, I'm the Chief of Staff here. I have no authority"?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never came to that point in any of our conversations. We never came to discuss that issue, and, after all, General Halilovic never needed to explain that to me. I never heard such an utterance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I want to quickly take you to the IKM command. Several questions were put to you by learned counsel for the Defence where he suggested to you that IKM was merely a location. Now, could you explain to us as to why there was a need, if you know, of course, to set up an IKM in Jablanica. Why was the operation not commanded from Sarajevo? After all Delic was in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, forward command posts were established normally only for one particular purpose, to be closer to the forces executing the mission, to be closer to the forces on the ground. If you were commanding forces from Sarajevo, you would be deprived of direct insight because our means of communication were pretty outdated, even obsolete, and messages took some time to arrive; whereas, the situation on the ground required quick response, quick reaction, and decision-making, and in such cases it was always justified and reasonable to set up a forward command post to command and control the activities. The forward command itself can be a facility from which you command and control. It is not a stable facility where personnel is based, normally, in addition to effective command and control. So by definition, the forward command post is smaller than a command. It contains only as much personnel and equipment as is necessary to effect these functions of control and command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in having such senior officers at this forward command post, it is quite plausible then to say that it had the full command authority, given the reasons about the lack of communications and things from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. They had the necessary experience and knowledge to effect successful command and control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'd like to quickly take you to breaches of military discipline and -- and crimes committed by -- by soldiers. Now, again, it was put to you that there are various lines of -- of military security and different levels at which -- a chain, as it were, as to who takes different kinds of actions in any breaches of discipline or any crimes committed by subordinates. Now, can you please in this respect tell me that -- what are the duplicates of a commander in respect of before, during, and after crimes being committed. Let's say, before you go into combat, what is a commander in respect of crimes or possible crimes being committed by subordinates? Secondly, what are your duties of a commander as the crimes are being committed? And then after, what are the duties of a commander? This is notwithstanding, of course, that there are other organs and institutions which are also seized of this -- of some duties in this respect. And I'm sorry it's a very long question, Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I'll try to answer it. Before --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before combat operations begin, commanders need to address the troops invoking international convenance, investigations, et cetera. During combat operation, they are required to cot the -- control the conduct of their troops. And if any role or international regulation is violated, they are required to take appropriate measures. That means to identify and locate the perpetrator of the violation in question and to institute disciplinary proceedings. Disciplinary proceedings are solely within the competence of commanders. And if criminal charges are pending, then professional bodies were available to help out, and the head of the professional authority would conduct this to the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the duty of the commander himself, now, what -- what would his duty be under these circumstances, when a crime has been committed? What would he do in practical terms, Mr. Gusic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practical terms, the commander institutes an investigation. He starts an investigation within his purview, within the framework of his powers. We have a two-pronged system: One problem is the disciplinary proceedings; and another one is criminal charges. If it is only disciplinary proceedings, then the commander is able to handle that by himself. If criminal charges are involved, then professional services need to collect evidence on the ground, create a picture of the event or, rather, reconstruct it, write a report, and depending on where the unit is, a decision is made whether to implement the punitive measure against the perpetrator immediately or to delay it until a later time. The duty of the commander in this case is to make sure that all the evidence in the case is preserved and to locate and isolate the perpetrators as soon as possible in order to hand them over to the professional authorities in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. Now, what would a duty of a commander be if he becomes aware that soldiers are committing crimes? They're happening. Soldiers under your command are committing crimes. What is the duties of a commander in that event?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such a commander, if it is practically possible to start an investigation, should start an investigation. If that is practically impossible, then he should seek help on is that score. But in any case, he should inform his superior of the occurrence because that's an extraordinary event, and according to our regulations, information has to be passed on vertically through the chain of command within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, perhaps you didn't quite understand my question. Your soldiers -- I'll give you a hypothetical -- are at the moment -- you're in the theatre of war. You get information your soldiers are killing some civilians. They're doing it right now. What do you do?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very categoric action needs to be taken. Forces need to be engaged immediately to stop this and prevent further killing, prevent the continuation of such activities, without any delay. The closest troops at hand should be engaged and sent there to stop any violation of the prevailing rules and regulations, and, of course, that involves locating, detecting, isolating perpetrators, and starting further proceedings. But the first step is to stop the violation, to minimise, contain the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then in that case, writing a report and reporting to your superiors would not be the option, would it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report can be filed within 24 hours. But if the reaction is late, then the damage eventually caused could be far greater than would have been the case if an earlier response had been secured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. Now, I want to ask you -- counsel for the Defence had asked you whether you'd seen any orders signed by Sefer Halilovic signed in his capacity both as Chief of Staff and as deputy commander. And to that end, I'd like to show you two documents. One is MFI161, Your Honour. And the 65 ter number was 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is that enough identification for you, court orderly? And 01805261. And the other one I want to show you is MFI123, and it's -- that's it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this document. That's one of the documents that I saw earlier. You showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns the engagement of the forces of the 1st Corps. Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, and below that it says "Assistant commander." Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I want to take you to the signature page, Mr. Gusic, please. And is that signed by Sefer Halilovic in his capacity as deputy commander and Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next document too. Could you also look at that. And I'm not sure if I'm going too fast for you, Mr. -- Mr. Ram.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is that on the ELMO? I can't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also look at the signature page of that.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it yet. I'm still looking at the first document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you call it a resubordination order? It's a bit leading, Your Honour. I'm just keeping eye on the time. If it's not, you'll correct me.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the order I mentioned before, resubordinating units from one larger unit to another larger unit or, alternatively, making previously independent units part of a larger unit. For instance, the Handzar Division becomes part of the special purpose unit Zulfikar. It is certainly a resubordination order. It should have been drafted properly by establishment, but it can be said that this is an organisational order as well, depending on -- on how you look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please look at the signature. Is this also signed by Sefer Halilovic in his capacity as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Chief of Staff of the Supreme Commander and deputy commander."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other question is about investigations of crimes, or that was the Defence counsel's heading anyway. It's in relation to document D623. I don't necessarily have to show it to you, unless you want to refresh your memory, but there it said -- this was a document where it basically was giving information that crimes were being committed by the BH army in Grabovica, and counsel for the Defence had put to you at the time that there were detainees who had been passing. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. It is a handwritten document drafted by the assistant from the 43rd Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the information in that document was that the Army of the BH had committed these crimes. There was nowhere in that document where it said the detainees had committed crimes. Would you like to refresh yourself or -- or do you think you can answer that question?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that document does not state that a crime had been committed. It says "there are indications that a crime may have been committed," meaning unverified information pointing to the possibility, et cetera. But I don't think that the context supports the assumption that it was done by the detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I stand corrected. Yes, purported and -- of crimes. Mr. Gusic, you cannot confirm, can you, where Mr. Halilovic was on the 8th and 9th of September, can you, from your own knowledge of his movements?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I cannot confirm a single date with any amount of certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mid-September generally would you -- was he at Konjic, according to your own information?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Halilovic was in early September, mid-September, and late September there, according to my information, but I do not contest any document that may come from the archives of the BH army that would run counter to this. As I told you at the outset, I cannot confirm any dates after so much time has passed. We can talk only about periods. Yes, early September, mid-September, late September, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. Gusic --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is in respect of MFI157. This was the document learned counsel for the Defence showed you, and this was about -- reassess the situation, the genocide committed in Grabovica, et cetera. Do you remember that particular order addressed to the Supreme Command Staff -- I mean, to the IK command and to yourself?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you'd never seen that document. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I had seen the document in that form. I can't remember seeing it. But I know the contents of the document. I'm aware of it because later on I had a talk with my Chief of Staff about why he had done it. I can't visualise the document, in other words, but that particular piece of information and the fact that it was something relayed by my Chief of Staff to the commander outside proper channels is something that stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who was it primarily addressed to? You -- it was -- you said it was to you for information, but who was the addressee who had to take action on that particular order?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the action stems from a chain of events that predates that order. The order was to revise the decision that had been taken earlier. I think it had to be sent to General Halilovic. If a certain crime had been committed, then the person in whose zone of responsibility it occurred had to be involved. The superior commander in that area, along that axis, was General Halilovic, so on both counts it should have been addressed to him. But I have to repeat: It was not usual in correspondence to submit a copy of such a document to underlings as well. That document should not have reached me, but maybe the commander decided to send it to me as well simply because my Chief of Staff provided the information in the first place. Perhaps my Chief of Staff would be better placed to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was General Halilovic who had to act on it; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear the interpretation. Yes. Yes, that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Chana. Witness, you mentioned that you would like to say something to this Bench. We still have two minutes left. You may say whatever you like at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have actually said it already. As I mentioned, I should have said it at the outset yesterday, the bit about Mr. Asim Dzambasovic. That is something I heard last year from Mr. Dautovic, who told me that Mr. Dzambasovic had attempted to take a statement from him reflecting different circumstances to those that actually happened in Prozor. Mr. Dzambasovic was one of the participants in that meeting, and I confirmed -- I cannot confirm that this was his precise establishment position but he was a commander of the operative group, an intelligence officer in the Prozor Battalion. Later when Mr. Dautovic declined to give this false statement, his wife was harassed by a young later whom they didn't know by the name of Edina or something like that, and Mr. Dautovic's wife was told that she can have the telephone number of the Prosecutor. I don't understand exactly what this insinuation was about. Briefly, I got this information from Mr. Dautovic before I met with Mr. Dzambasovic. And when I finally met him, I said, "I am not going to say hello or shake hands with people who stoop to such things." A couple of days later, one of my superiors invited me to a conference and told me that I shouldn't have acted like that with Mr. Dzambasovic. Mr. Dzambasovic went to so far as to address a very insulting letter to my commander, a letter insulting to me, but this letter led me to ask to be relieved of my duties in the army of the Federation after 26 years of service because I did not wish to stay in the ranks of an army which was subject to influence by such unsavoury individuals, and I saw the map that Mr. Dzambasovic produced. I believe it was tendentiously made, and it does not reflect the information, the facts I remember from the conference in Zenica. It doesn't say anywhere "inclusive of" or "exclusive of. And for your information, Your Honours, "exclusive" in our terms means that a certain unit is obliged to also provide security for a particular feature or facility, and if you write "exclusively," that means that security falls within somebody else's competence. I emphatically claimed, therefore, that the map later made by Mr. Dzambasovic does not reflect the reality because he arrogated the right to add words "inclusive" or "exclusive." This is what I wanted to get off my chest, and I'm sorry if this led to some bad blood. I tried to answer questions honestly, in good faith, and I am prepared to accept any responsibility that I may rightly be subject to, and I can only say what I've already mentioned before: Everything that a person has to leave behind are good deeds and good words or, alternatively, bad deeds and bad words. This is what I wanted to leave behind me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I just have one question to ask you: Did you tell this information to the Prosecution team before testifying this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I shared this information with the Office of the Prosecutor. I cannot tell you the exact date, but it was at the time when I was reviewing the DVD. I made a copy of the letter at that time and gave it to Mr. Brun, and I can show you that letter. I have it with me. I gave them this letter. However, I had no detailed conversation with the Prosecutor about this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll certainly look into this matter. Thank you. Well, at this moment, we have two lists of the documents that both parties would like to tender at this stage, but it seems to me that we could not do it for today, so I hope that the parties could write a very concise motion challenging the admission of each other's documents in two days. Maybe we have to do it in written form. I'm very sorry to say that this is the last result we would like to use, but since we are constrained by the time limits, we have to do that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to make sure that I understand Your Honour as well, this is with respect to the documents to be tendered just by this witness alone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, by this witness alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I hope that my -- the Defence counsel team would be mindful that some of the documents they used themselves, to take that into consideration when they're doing their motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course. Of course. Well, witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your testimony, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home, and I apologise for having kept you here for so long. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
